summary: The note lists the top 10 mistakes people make when disposing of household chemicals, drawing on interviews with local residents and experts such as Mary Goldsmith and Richard Banks. Mistakes include flushing, trashing, stockpiling, ignoring labels, pouring oil down drains, mixing chemicals, and mishandling electronics, batteries, and plastics. It urges residents to use community hazardous waste resources and change their habits to prevent soil, air, and water pollution.
one_line: A local guide to the top 10 household chemical disposal mistakes and how to dispose of hazardous items sustainably.
key_facts: As of September 23, 2023, the community had growing concern about improper disposal of household chemicals, which can contaminate soil, air, and water.
Mary Goldsmith is founder of GreenHouse, a local environmental advocacy group; Richard Banks is a senior waste management coordinator for the city.

Richard Banks observed on October 1, 2023 that many households still flush chemicals such as old medication and paints down toilets or drains, though wastewater treatment plants cannot filter out all chemical contaminants.

Jane Peters, a resident, confessed on October 10, 2023 to throwing expired cosmetics and cleaning products in her kitchen garbage; landfills are not equipped for hazardous waste and seepage can contaminate ground and water.
Mike Clarkson found a garage cabinet full of half-used products accumulated over decades in September 2023, an example of stockpiling that leads to overwhelming, improper disposal later.
Mary Goldsmith said at a September 15, 2023 seminar that disregarding label disposal instructions is one of the gravest homeowner mistakes.
Cooking oil and grease poured down the sink can solidify in pipes and cause blockages and harm aquatic life; it should be stored in a container and disposed of per local guidelines.
Hardware store owner Tom Nicholson reported on October 20, 2023 a customer mixing different paints; mixing chemicals can cause dangerous reactions or toxic gases.
A local university study on September 30, 2023 advised taking electronics to specialized e-waste recycling centers.

A local battery recycling initiative said on October 5, 2023 that batteries can leak toxic chemicals like cadmium and lead, and should go to battery recycling programs, not the trash or recycling bin.
A local recycling plant operator clarified on October 12, 2023 that not all plastics are recyclable, as chemical residue or material type can contaminate recycling streams.
A local council meeting on October 25, 2023 identified that many residents are unaware of or don't use hazardous waste collection centers and scheduled collection days.
